extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on evaluating obviousness rejections, weighing rebuttal evidence, secondary considerations (nexus), and the applicability of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) disqualifications during patent examination and appeal. Covers admissible evidence, common argument pitfalls, and legal standards/case law to apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight to accord rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence presented in a timely manner should not be ignored but need not be accorded the same weight; examiners must determine the relative weight of rebuttal evidence (e.g., nexus, commensurateness with the claimed invention). An obviousness rejection should be made or maintained only if evidence of obviousness outweighs evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether a nexus exists between the claimed invention and the proffered evidence and whether the evidence is commensurate in scope with the claimed invention. The standard is the 'preponderance of the evidence' (see MPEP §706). The mere presence of some credible rebuttal evidence does not automatically require withdrawal of an obviousness rejection. See MPEP §716.01(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of nexus and nexus requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A presumption of nexus may arise where marketed products are coextensive with the claims, but coextensiveness alone does not decide the overall nexus question; objective evidence lacks nexus if it exclusively relates to a feature 'known in the prior art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate nexus using MPEP §716.01(b) guidance. When secondary considerations are tied only to an element that the prior art disclosed, nexus may be lacking. Case example: Yita LLC v. MacNeil IP LLC (Fed. Cir. 2023) — Board's presumption and nexus findings reversed when nexus rested on legal errors. Ensure secondary consideration evidence is linked to the claimed invention as a whole, not solely to a feature known in the prior art. See Rambus v. Rea and WBIP v. Kohler guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant argument is not evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An argument by the applicant is not evidence unless it is an admission; arguments cannot take the place of factual evidence in the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant assertions present factual matters, they must be supported by appropriate affidavits or declarations under the cited rules (see MPEP §§2155, 715 et seq., 716 et seq., and 37 CFR 1.130–1.132). See In re De Blauwe; In re Schulze; In re Geisler. See MPEP §716.01(c) for examples of applicant statements that are not evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of additional advantages/latent properties does not rebut prima facie obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere recognition of latent properties or additional advantages present but not recognized in the prior art does not render an otherwise known invention nonobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery of an inherent or latent function that would 'flow naturally' from the prior art cannot form the basis for patentability if the differences would otherwise be obvious. Case examples: In re Wiseman; In re Baxter Travenol Labs.; Ex parte Obiaya; Lantech v. Kaufman. See MPEP §716.02–§716.02(g) for unexpected result/declaratory evidence discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical combinability not required to combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: A determination of obviousness based on multiple references does not require actual physical substitution of elements; the test is whether the combined teachings would have suggested the claimed invention to a PHOSITA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Mouttet, In re Etter, In re Keller, In re Sneed, In re Nievelt. However, the claimed combination cannot change the principle of operation of the primary reference or render it inoperable for its intended purpose (see MPEP §2143.01 VI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot show nonobviousness by attacking references individually when rejection is based on combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Attacking individual references is insufficient where the rejection is based on a combination; the reply must address the combined teachings and suggestions of the applied prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant's reply establishes that each applied reference fails to teach a limitation and addresses the combined teachings, reliance on Keller is not appropriate. See In re Keller, In re Merck & Co., and In re Mouttet. Examiners should evaluate the combined suggestion to a PHOSITA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of references combined is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on a large number of references in a rejection does not, by itself, weigh against the obviousness of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A combination using many references can still render claims obvious. Case example: In re Gorman (thirteen references sustaining rejection). Focus on whether the combined teachings would have motivated combination and rendered the claim obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import unclaimed limitations from the specification into claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Although claims are interpreted in light of the specification, limitations from the specification are not read into the claims unless compelled by the intrinsic record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe claims to include specification-only limitations absent clear evidence that the patentee intended those limitations to define the claim scope. Case examples: In re Van Geuns; Constant v. AMD; Ex parte McCullough. See MPEP §§2111–2116.01 for claim interpretation law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/business considerations do not establish nonobviousness absent technological incompatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that a combination would not be made by businesspeople for economic reasons do not establish that a PHOSITA would not make the combination unless technological incompatibility would prevent it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the reason preventing combination is technological rather than economic. Case example: In re Farrenkopf. Examiners should not accept pure economic infeasibility as proof of nonobviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age of references is not persuasive without evidence of tried-and-failed history
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere age of prior art references does not establish unobviousness absent evidence that the art tried and failed to solve the problem despite knowledge of the references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Older references may still be relied upon if there is no evidence that one skilled in the art tried and failed. Case examples: In re Wright; Ex parte Meyer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement (nonanalogous art argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a reference is analogous art is a relevant consideration for obviousness analysis (see MPEP §2141.01(a) for case law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the prior art is from the same field of endeavor or reasonably pertinent to the problem addressed by the inventor. Use §2141.01(a) guidance and supporting case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impermissible hindsight caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may argue examiner conclusions are based on improper hindsight reasoning; reconstruction is permitted only if it relies on knowledge within the level of ordinary skill at the time and not on the applicant's disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of ex post reasoning and hindsight bias; KSR permits reconstruction that uses only contemporaneous knowledge and common sense. See In re McLaughlin; KSR Int’l Co. v. Teleflex; relevant Federal Circuit caution about hindsight. Assess whether claimed motivation to combine relies on post hoc knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious‑to‑try rationale — when it supports obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'obvious to try' rationale may support obviousness where a PHOSITA is choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply KSR factors: if prior art identifies a finite set of predictable options and a PHOSITA would have had a reasonable expectation of success, 'obvious to try' can show obviousness. Counterexamples where it should not apply include when prior art gives no indication which parameters are critical or the technology is exploratory. See KSR and In re O’Farrell. Use caution distinguishing proper vs improper 'obvious to try' applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of explicit suggestion/TSM is not fatal to an obviousness finding
rubrics_metrics.description: A teaching, suggestion, or motivation (TSM) to combine references in the prior art is an appropriate rationale, but it is only one of multiple valid rationales consistent with KSR for concluding obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider alternative rationales identified by KSR (common sense, market forces, design incentives, known interchangeable elements, etc.). See MPEP §§2141 and 2143 for guidance on establishing a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away doctrine — nature and weight matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference that 'teaches away' from the claimed invention is significant evidence in determining obviousness, but the substance and degree of the teaching away must be weighed; mere preference does not equal teaching away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the prior art criticizes, discredits, or discourages the claimed solution. References that merely disclose multiple alternatives or express general preference do not necessarily teach away. Case examples: In re Gurley; In re Fulton; UCB v. Actavis; Schwendimann v. Neenah. If references expressly teach away from combination, combining them may be improper (see In re Grasselli).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceeding contrary to accepted wisdom can indicate nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claimed approach proceeds contrary to accepted wisdom in the art, that fact is evidence supporting nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider totality of prior art; known disadvantages that would discourage searching for new inventions may be relevant. Case example: In re Hedges; United States v. Adams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of KSR across technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: KSR's principles apply across technologies, including fields historically deemed 'unpredictable' such as biotechnology; rejections should not be withdrawn solely because the field is unpredictable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess obviousness using KSR functional approach regardless of technological field. See In re Kubin and MPEP §2143.02. Do not 'cabin' KSR to only predictable arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability and use of form paragraphs for examiner responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraphs (e.g., MPEP §707.07(f) form paragraphs 7.37–7.38) may be used where applicant’s arguments are not persuasive or are moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners may use approved form paragraphs when appropriate, but should ensure the substantive basis for the decision is recorded and tailored as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — general disqualification rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter developed by another that qualifies as prior art only under certain subsections of 102 may be disqualified from consideration under 103 where the subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment at the time the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre‑AIA 103(c) applies only to obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) and only to prior art qualifying under subsections (e), (f), or (g) (depending on era/amendments). It does not apply to rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 or to double patenting rejections. The applicant bears the burden of establishing disqualification. See MPEP §2146 and §2146.02 for procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: CREATE Act/joint research agreement disqualification conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the CREATE Act, subject matter developed by another is treated as owned (thus disqualified) for purposes of 103 if three conditions are met: (A) invention made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) invention made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the patent application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these three statutory conditions for 'joint research agreement disqualification' when examining pre‑AIA prior art under 103. See statutory text and MPEP §2146 and §2146.01 for applicability timing (dates of enactment and patent grant matter for which version applies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and timing rules for pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicability of pre‑AIA 103(c) depends on filing/grant dates and amendments (1999 AIPA, 2004 CREATE Act): which versions apply depends on application filing date and patent grant date; the provision only disqualifies prior art that falls within its covered subsections and temporal scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective Nov 29, 1999 and Dec 10, 2004 amendments changed which prior art (e.g., 102(e)) could be disqualified and for which patents/applications. For reexamination, determine whether the patent was granted on/after Dec 10, 2004. See MPEP §2146 for detailed applicability rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of disclosure and duties for applications with related foreign filings or joint inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants who combine subject matter from related applications or name joint inventors must disclose invention dates and common ownership information under 37 CFR 1.56; absent contrary evidence, examiners assume compliance with duty of disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign applicants combining related applications should provide invention dates and ownership information to enable examiner consideration of potential 103(a) rejections based on 102(f)/(g). For inventions not commonly owned at the time of invention, claims in a single application are not shielded from 103(a) rejections based on that prior art. See MPEP §2146.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use affidavits/declarations to rebut prior art rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.130, 1.131, or 1.132 may be used to overcome prior art rejections where appropriate (see MPEP §§2155; 715 et seq.; 716 et seq.; 2136.05 references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the specific MPEP sections for which rule applies to the circumstance (e.g., 1.130 timely evidence, 1.131 late evidence, 1.132 evidence in AIA/pre‑AIA contexts). Ensure affidavits/declarations provide the factual support necessary to rebut a prima facie case and satisfy requirements for admissibility and weight.
